text: Fluconazole is a moderate inhibitor of CYP2C9.
Fluconazole is used to treat candidiasis and cryptococcal meningitis.
Fluconazole has high oral bioavailability, close to 90%.
Fluconazole is eliminated predominantly unchanged in the urine.
Fluconazole can prolong the QT interval at high doses.
Warfarin's more potent S-enantiomer is metabolised by CYP2C9.
Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist used for anticoagulation.
Warfarin therapy is monitored by INR.
Warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index.
Warfarin is highly bound to plasma albumin.

Yes. Fluconazole is a moderate inhibitor of CYP2C9, and warfarin's more potent S-enantiomer is metabolised by CYP2C9. Inhibiting this enzyme reduces S-warfarin clearance, raising plasma levels of the active enantiomer and increasing anticoagulant effect. Because warfarin has a narrow therapeutic index, even a moderate reduction in metabolism can push patients above the therapeutic range, raising bleeding risk. This is a pharmacokinetic interaction (metabolic inhibition), not a pharmacodynamic one, and it is clinically significant — INR monitoring and possible warfarin dose reduction are warranted during co-prescription. The other listed fluconazole properties (renal elimination, high bioavailability, QT prolongation) do not alter this conclusion.

MECHANISM: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, decreasing metabolism of the potent S-enantiomer of warfarin, increasing warfarin exposure
FINAL ANSWER: YES
